title: Samarra
summary: Samarra, on the Tigris in Iraq, served as the Abbasid capital from 836 to 892, after al-Mu'tasim left Baghdad. Its large mosques, palaces and spiral minaret, plus the Samarra stucco style and Lustre Ware, spread across the Islamic world. UNESCO inscribed the archaeological city in 2007.

as_recorded.value: In 836, when the Abbasid caliph al-Muʿtaṣim was pressured to leave Baghdad
In 892 the caliph al-Muʿtamid transferred the capital back to Baghdad
The ancient capital of Samarra dating from 836-892

importance.justification: Short-lived but best-preserved Abbasid capital, source of influential architectural and artistic styles.

reviewer_note: Dates are the capital period 836-892; the site has older prehistoric settlement per Britannica. Sources differ on the extent: UNESCO gives 41.5 km, Britannica says the town stretched 20 miles (32 km). Britannica says the town was founded between the 3rd and 7th centuries CE.
